euphoria

yoo-FOR-ee-uh -- four syllables, stress on the second syllable, FOR. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Euphoria is a feeling of intense excitement and happiness.

A wave of euphoria swept through mission control when the rover's signal finally returned.

Example

She crosses the marathon's finish line, and for ten dizzy minutes of pure euphoria the soreness simply does not exist -- she is laughing, hugging strangers, floating somewhere above the pavement.

Euphoria is that flood of feeling: intense excitement and happiness, usually brief and overwhelming while it lasts. It is the peak itself -- higher than being elated, and far too intense to be anyone's everyday mood.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bliss: Bliss is perfect, serene happiness -- calm, quiet, and glad to last forever. Euphoria is joy at the opposite tempo: a racing, electric high that floods in fast, overwhelms everything, and is usually gone within minutes.

glee: Glee is bright, bubbling delight at a small win or a bit of mischief -- you can rub your hands with glee. Euphoria is far larger: an overwhelming flood of happiness that sweeps through your whole body.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

despair: the complete loss of hope

misery: great unhappiness or suffering

Where it sits · how overwhelming the happiness is — delight → euphoria → rapture

delight vs. euphoria: Delight is the gentle, weaker cousin -- a good dessert or a clever joke brings a moment of delight -- while euphoria is a tidal wave: happiness so intense it briefly crowds out everything else.

rapture vs. euphoria: Rapture goes a step further than euphoria: euphoria races through you, but rapture carries you away entirely, so absorbing that the world outside the joy disappears.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — eu-

prefix — eu-: good, well (Greek)

root — phor-

root — phor-: to bear, to carry (Greek pherein)

suffix — -ia

suffix — -ia: state or condition of (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Euphoria is Greek for 'bearing well' -- eu- ('good, well') plus pherein ('to carry'). Doctors once used it for a patient carrying an illness comfortably; today it names the state of being carried high by intense excitement and happiness.

Use the root in a new word: metaphor

Use the root in a new word: metaphor: Calling the noisy classroom 'a zoo' is a metaphor -- it carries one idea across to describe another.

Root Check

Word Choice

Euphoria is a noun for the peak itself, and it rarely lasts: a wave of euphoria, the euphoria faded. Elated is the adjective for a person riding a high; euphoria is the high. If the feeling is quiet or long-lasting, reach for contentment instead -- euphoria always races.
